transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-07-07
Start time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Kapoor (Redwood SE), Elena Martinez (Oxbow Head of Platform), Tom Liu (Oxbow SRE), Priya Nair (Oxbow Finance)

Summary:
Quick console-first walkthrough focusing on per-path / per-route usage visibility, cost decomposition by model & route, and how Redwood Optimize recommendations can reduce unit cost (batching, prefix caching, quantization profiles). Customer asked questions about private deployments, SOC 2 logs, and how to map their internal route names to Redwood routes. Agreed to run a 48hr benchmark and exchange traffic traces; next meeting to align pilot scope.

Topics covered:
- Overview of Usage Fabric (per-route telemetry + tag mapping)
- Route-level cost breakdown (token + model compute)
- Quick demo: filtering by tag, time window, and SLA buckets
- Optimize recommendations: batching, KV/prefix caching and quantization suggestions
- Deployment options: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC) and tradeoffs
- Security / compliance: SOC 2 reports, KMS, SSO/SAML, audit logs
- Pilot scoping and benchmarks

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood Inference team, and with me is Ravi our solutions engineer. Real quick intros?
[00:07] Elena: Elena here, head of platform at Oxbow. We focus on inference for document understanding across our supply chain configs.
[00:11] Tom: Tom, SRE. I'll be the one actually running any tests and looking at latency numbers.
[00:14] Priya: Priya, finance. I'll be looking at unit economics and licensing.
[00:18] Ravi: Great, thanks. Quick agenda — we want to show the console usage fabric, per-route dashboards, and a cost breakdown. Then talk about pilot and security. Sound good?
[00:26] Elena: Yes. We're mostly interested in: 1) how do we map our internal routes to yours, 2) how we can see cost per endpoint and user, and 3) how much we save if we move to Dedicated pools.
[00:37] Maya: Perfect. I'll share my screen — give me a sec.
[00:42] [screen share noise]
[00:45] Maya: Ok, this is the Usage Fabric dashboard. At the top you can see aggregate traffic — tokens in, tokens out — and a breakdown by model. The left rail is filters: service tags, route name, team, time window.
[00:56] Tom: Looks like you do a model-level split — is that exact or inferred? I see 'redwood-recommended-3b' and such.
[01:03] Ravi: Good question. The dashboard shows the model variant that actually served the request; sometimes we route to a 'compatible variant' — so you may see a few names. The telemetry maps the chosen kernel/model to cost and latency. Occasionally the auto-naming gets messy in transcription — you might see 'redwood reco three bee' on the raw logs, but we store canonical model ids too.
[01:22] Elena: How do we attach our internal route names? We have product names like /api/v1/annotate or customers ops flows with internal tags.
[01:28] Maya: You can push tags via the SDK header or use our route mapping UI. If you send a x-redwood-route header we surface it as route name. For existing traffic we can do a mapping job with your traces.
[01:39] Priya: From finance perspective, can you break costs per route and per team? We have shared models across teams so we need to allocate.
[01:46] Ravi: Yes — route-level cost breakdown is one of the core views. You can drill from model->route->user. We calculate compute cost per token + provisioned pool amortization. For Dedicated we amortize the reserved capacity over usage windows.
[01:58] Maya: I'll pull up a sample route view — here we have Route A, Route B. Notice Route A has high TTI (time to inference) because it's hitting a larger model for long prompts. We surface 95th percentile latency and p50 so SREs can tune.
[02:12] [crosstalk] Tom: When you say amortize — do you mean you show both nominal per-token cost and effective cost accounting for reserved capacity?
[02:18] Ravi: Exactly. On the right column we show two cost columns: 'incremental cost' (what you pay per token on hosted) and 'effective cost' (after reserved capacity amortization and any platform discounts).
[02:27] Elena: Do you show batch sizes or batching stats? I've read Redwood has continuous batching — how visible is that to us?
[02:33] Ravi: We surface the average batch size for a given route and time window. Also the latency impact of batching — a latency vs throughput curve for the route. That makes it easier to pick SLO points.
[02:45] Priya: And the Optimize tab — does it give concrete recommendations? Like 'increase max batch to 8' or 'enable KV caching for prefix X'?
[02:53] Ravi: Yes, Optimize recommendations are prescriptive. Example: for Route A we suggest prefix caching because a lot of requests share the same context — that'll lower per-token compute by X%. We also show simulation of cost impact if you change batch or quantization.
[03:08] Elena: Quantization — is that automatic or do you onboard model variants? We use a finetuned model in-house.
[03:13] Ravi: For finetuned or private models, we offer quantization profiles and recommend variants for serving. For hosted open models we have prebuilt quantized variants. For private deployments, we work with your team to evaluate accuracy vs q-int. There's human-in-the-loop evals to catch regressions.
[03:29] Tom: Security question — we need SOC 2, SSO, and KMS integration. Also audit logs for token-level tracing. How mature are those features?
[03:36] Maya: Redwood is SOC 2 Type II compliant — we'll share the attestation. For SSO we support SAML/Okta — and RBAC at the route and project level. For encryption, we integrate with customer KMS for Private deployments; in Hosted we encrypt at rest with our managed keys but can do Bring-Your-Own-Key for VPC/Private. Audit logs include request ids and the model variant, though transcripts are not stored unless you opt in.
[03:58] Priya: Ok good. Are the audit logs exportable to our SIEM?
[04:02] Ravi: Yes, we can ship logs to S3 or a customer ELK/Datadog forwarder.
[04:07] Elena: About data retention — we need 90 days of telemetry for compliance.
[04:11] Maya: We can configure retention windows in the Private control plane; hosted defaults are 30/90 for telemetry and 365 for billing. We'll share the exact retention policies in the security packet.
[04:22] [pause]
[04:26] Maya: Back to the demo — I'm going to click into a per-route breakdown. Note the waterfall chart: tokens -> model compute -> infra overhead -> caching delta. You can toggle to show token counts or dollars.
[04:40] Tom: Can I export that to CSV for our chargeback tool?
[04:42] Ravi: Yes, everything is exportable via API and there's a billing export that maps route->cost center.
[04:48] Elena: What about multi-region traffic? Some of our flows need APAC residency.
[04:53] Maya: We support region routing. For Hosted we have regional endpoints; for Dedicated or Private you can provision in the region. The routing policy can pin requests to region, and our console shows region-level cost differences.
[05:03] Tom: Great. One more on performance — what's the expected 95th percentile for a 2k token prompt on your dedicated M-60 equivalent?
[05:10] Ravi: Ballpark: for a quantized 7B-ish open model on a Dedicated A100-style pool we see 95p around 180–250ms per token depending on context caching. For larger models it's higher. But we'll put precise numbers in the benchmark we're running.
[05:23] Maya: I'm going to demo Optimize simulation — clicking simulate: we changed batch size from 1->8 and enabled prefix caching. It predicts a 38% reduction in per-token compute and a slight increase in 95p latency for the heaviest route.
[05:38] Priya: That projection is interesting. Does simulation take into account our traffic skews?
[05:42] Ravi: Yes, if we ingest the traces we can run the simulation on real traffic. That's why we asked for sample traces.
[05:48] Elena: Ok, next how do we start a pilot? We want a week on Dedicated with a canary route, then scale if the numbers look good.
[05:56] Maya: Typical pilot flow: 1) we provision a small Dedicated pool, 2) we onboard 1–2 routes and run a 48hr throughput + latency benchmark, 3) we run cost sim and compare with current hosted per-token costs, 4) decide on commit.
[06:10] Tom: What are minimum commits for Dedicated?
[06:12] Maya: Depends on SKU — we'll send you the SKU sheet. There's also burst capacity if you need temporary headroom.
[06:18] Priya: Any discounts for an annual commit?
[06:20] Maya: Yes, standard reserved capacity discounts apply — we'll include examples in the pricing sheet.
[06:26] Elena: Any red flags we should know about? The main one for us is accuracy regressions when switching quantization.
[06:31] Ravi: We guard against that with eval harnesses: you provide prompt/eval sets and we run automated quality checks and threshold alerts. If quantization causes regressions we can pin to a full-precision variant or tune the q profile.
[06:42] [background noise]
[06:45] Maya: Ok, quick live example — I've added a filter 'team: document-qa' and time window last 7 days. You can see Route 'annotate_v2' is the largest spend. Click Insights -> Cost Drivers shows that 65% of cost is model compute and 20% is infra overhead (provisioning).
[06:59] Tom: Could we surface per-customer spend under that route? We do per-customer chargebacks.
[07:04] Ravi: Yes, we support dimensions: route, team, customer_id. If your customer_id is in request headers we map and break out cost per customer.
[07:12] Elena: For the mapping job — what's the cadence? We want daily reconciliation with our billing.
[07:16] Maya: Billing exports can be daily, and there's a reconciliation API.
[07:19] Priya: Regarding legal and procurement — what's the procurement lead time for Private deployment? We might need on-prem or VPC for certain customers.
[07:26] Maya: Private deployment lead times vary — for a VPC it's a few weeks; on-prem longer depending on infra. We'll surface a checklist and the support plan needed.
[07:34] Tom: One more technical — how does KV cache behave across restarts? We sometimes have evictions.
[07:39] Ravi: KV/prefix caching persists in the serving layer for the lifetime of the instance; for Dedicated there's warmup options and persistent caches for steady traffic. We also support cache snapshotting for quick warm-up after scale events. Eviction policies are LRU by default.
[07:54] Elena: Are there any limits on event-level retention in audit logs for compliance?
[07:58] Maya: We can configure retention up to configurable windows; for Hosted it's configurable up to a limit, but Private gives you full control. We'll include retention options in the security packet.
[08:07] [silence]
[08:10] Maya: Ok, wrapping up — recap of what we agreed: Ravi will run a benchmark using the sample traces; Maya will send pricing and security docs; Oxbow will provide sample traffic and critical route list. Then we'll schedule a pilot kick-off.
[08:24] Elena: Sounds good. Can we get the security packet and pilot checklist by Friday?
[08:28] Maya: Yes — I'll send today or tomorrow.
[08:31] Priya: Also include examples of effective cost reduction scenarios — maybe a 3-route case study.
[08:35] Maya: Will do.
[08:37] [unintelligible]
[08:39] Tom: Quick note — when you run the benchmark, include a cold start and a warm start window; we want to see both.
[08:45] Ravi: Noted — we'll include cold/warm windows and p50/p95/p99 latency.
[08:50] Maya: Great. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with artifacts and a proposed pilot date for week of July 18.
[08:58] Elena: Thanks.
[09:00] Meeting end.

Post-meeting notes (auto):
- Security packet (SOC2, SAML, KMS docs) to be shared by Maya.
- Benchmark to include 48hr throughput, cold/warm windows, p50/p95/p99, and per-route cost breakdown.
- Simulation results will be generated using provided traces to estimate savings from batching + caching.

Recording quality notes: occasional transcription errors around model names and acronyms (e.g., 'K V cache' transcribed inconsistently). Some speakers overlap resulting in minor label mix-ups.
